records.old: When this leaf is cut and left without water, the chloroplasts cannot complete photosynthesis — the glucose supply drops — and the cell begins to starve. That is the beginning of the wilting we saw in Lesson 1.'
records.new: When this leaf is left in the sun and cut off from its roots, it loses water and cannot replace it. As the cells dry out, photosynthesis slows and the glucose supply drops, so the cell slowly starves. But the wilting you saw on Day 1 comes first, and the next card explains it.'
records.why: The old script said that stopping photosynthesis is 'the beginning of the wilting'. It is not. A leaf wilts first because its cells lose water and turgor pressure falls (taught in Lesson 4). Slower photosynthesis and starvation follow as cells dry out. The phenomenon is a leaf left IN the sun, so 'cut off from sunlight' was also wrong. Checked against the Lesson 4 chain: water loss -> shrinking vacuole -> lost turgor -> wilting; later: less glucose, less energy, cell death.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 30 'Plant Form and Physiology' (water potential, turgor pressure and wilting) and Chapter 5.2/5.3 (osmosis, tonicity)
records.group_headline: The explanation of the wilting leaf blamed starvation and 'no sunlight' for what is really water loss and lost turgor; the order of causes is now correct everywhere

records.why: Knock-on of the wilting-chain correction: the phenomenon is a leaf left in the sun, not one cut off from sunlight.

records.old: If the mitochondria stop working, the cell cannot release energy from glucose, so the plant cannot carry out active transport of water, and it wilts. If the chloroplasts stop working, the plant cannot photosynthesise and will starve
records.new: If the vacuole loses its water, turgor pressure falls and the cell goes limp, so the leaf wilts. If the chloroplasts stop working, the plant cannot photosynthesise and will slowly starve; if the mitochondria stop working, the cell cannot release energy from glucose and its other jobs fail
records.why: The model answer said wilting happens because mitochondria stop and 'active transport of water' fails. Water is not moved by active transport (it moves by osmosis), and wilting is caused by loss of turgor. Teachers use this answer as the standard for 'good', so it had to be right.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 5.2 (osmosis) and Chapter 30 (turgor pressure and wilting)

records.old: They articulated the causal chain: chloroplasts capture light energy → mitochondria release energy for cell processes → vacuole maintains turgor pressure → cell wall provides structural support → without these working together, the sukuma wiki leaf wilts, dries, and dies.
records.new: They articulated the causal chain: in the sun the leaf loses water → the vacuole shrinks and turgor pressure falls → the cell wall alone cannot hold the leaf up, so it wilts → as the cells dry out, chloroplasts can no longer make glucose and mitochondria can no longer release energy from it → the organelles stop working and the leaf dries and dies.
records.why: The old 'chain' listed organelle jobs one after another as if each caused the next. It did not explain why the leaf wilts. Replaced by the real order of causes.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 30 'Plant Form and Physiology'

records.old: the breakdown of chloroplasts to the failure of photosynthesis, and the cessation of mitochondrial activity to the inability of cells to release the energy needed for all life processes
records.new: the drying-out of the cells to the failure of photosynthesis and of mitochondrial energy release, so that the cells can no longer carry out life processes
records.why: The old wording said chloroplasts 'break down' first. In a leaf drying in the sun it is water loss that comes first; the organelles then fail because the cell dries out.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 30 'Plant Form and Physiology'

records.old: When the leaf is left in the sun, it loses water. The vacuole shrinks and turgor pressure falls. The cell wall alone cannot hold the leaf up, so it wilts. Without water the chloroplasts cannot carry out photosynthesis, so less glucose is made. The mitochondria then have less glucose from which to release energy, so the cell cannot power its life processes, and the organelles stop working.
records.new: When the leaf is left in the sun, it loses water to the hot air and, being a cut piece, cannot replace it. The vacuole shrinks and turgor pressure falls, so the vacuole no longer pushes the cell membrane against the cell wall. The cell wall alone cannot hold the leaf up, so it wilts. This comes first. As the cells dry out further, photosynthesis in the chloroplasts slows, so less glucose is made. The mitochondria then have less glucose from which to release energy, so the cell cannot power its life processes, and the organelles stop working.
records.why: A reviewer found the cause-and-effect chain thin. The chain is now in the correct order and states the mechanism (vacuole stops pushing the membrane against the wall) and that photosynthesis and respiration fail later because the cells dry out. This is the answer teachers compare learners against.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 30 'Plant Form and Physiology' (turgor pressure and wilting)
records.where: Final Explanation, Part 4: Why the leaf wilts and dies, exemplar

records.old: Say: 'Let us go back to our predictions board. Which of our predictions were correct? Which surprised you?'

Teacher notes on the limits of the Venn diagram (it shows what these micrographs show, and is a simplification): (1) if a learner asks whether plants have lysosomes, say plants do the same job of breaking down worn-out parts inside the vacuole, and that centrioles are found in animal cells but not in higher plants such as sukuma wiki; (2) animal cells can have small, temporary vacuoles, so it is the LARGE central vacuole that is plant-specific; (3) onion bulb cells have a cell wall and a large vacuole but NO chloroplasts (they are underground), so do not let learners record chloroplasts as present in every plant cell. Chloroplasts are shown in the sukuma wiki leaf (Image A and B).
records.why: The Venn diagram is the class's reference for 'what plant cells have that animal cells do not', and the Final Explanation relies on it. Three statements were over-simple: lysosomes are usually described as animal-cell structures but plant vacuoles do the same breaking-down job; animal cells may have small vacuoles; and the evidence sheet and column headings said 'Sukuma Wiki / Onion', yet onion bulb cells contain no chloroplasts. The teacher note keeps the Venn diagram usable and honest.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 4 'Cell Structure' (4.1 Studying cells; 4.3 Eukaryotic cells; 4.4 The endomembrane system; 4.5 Cytoskeleton)
records.group_headline: The plant/animal comparison hid three simplifications (lysosomes, centrioles, vacuoles) and the onion cells would have taught that plants always have chloroplasts

records.old: 'I am the gatekeeper — like the entry barrier at a Nairobi supermarket, I decide what enters and leaves the cell' [cell membrane]; 'I am the manager's office — I hold the master blueprint for every protein the cell will ever make' [nucleus]; 'I am the jiko — I break down glucose from ugali and githeri to release ATP energy the cell can use immediately' [mitochondria]; 'I am the postal sorting office at the Kisumu GPO — I package, label, and dispatch proteins to wherever they are needed' [Golgi apparatus]; 'I am the rigid fence around the homestead — I give the sukuma wiki cell its box-like shape and prevent it from bursting when the vacuole fills with water' [cell wall]; 'I am the water tank — when I am full, I press against the fence and keep the sukuma wiki leaf stiff and upright; when I empty, the leaf wilts' [large central vacuole]; 'I am the small workshop fundi — I read the blueprint and build every protein in the cell' [ribosome]; 'I am the delivery road from the manager's office to the postal sorting office — proteins travel along my folded membranes' [rough ER]
records.new: 'I am the security gate at the Mombasa port — I control what enters and leaves the cell' [cell membrane]; 'I am the County Governor's office — I hold the instructions for running the cell, including the plans for every protein it will ever make' [nucleus]; 'I am the jiko — I break down glucose from ugali and githeri to release ATP energy the cell can use immediately' [mitochondria]; 'I am the Nairobi GPO — I package, label, and dispatch proteins to wherever they are needed' [Golgi apparatus]; 'I am the rigid fence around the homestead — I give the sukuma wiki cell its box-like shape and prevent it from bursting when the vacuole fills with water' [cell wall]; 'I am the water tank — when I am full, I press against the fence and keep the sukuma wiki leaf stiff and upright; when I empty, the leaf wilts' [large central vacuole]; 'I am the small workshop fundi — I read the blueprint and build every protein in the cell' [ribosome]; 'I am the road network from the fundi's workshop to the delivery point — proteins made on the ribosomes stuck to me travel along my folded membranes' [rough ER]
records.why: Lesson 3 teaches: cell membrane = Mombasa port gate, nucleus = County Governor's office, Golgi = Nairobi GPO, rough ER = road network from the fundi's workshop (ribosomes) to the delivery point. The Lesson 5 cards used a supermarket barrier, 'the manager's office' and the 'Kisumu GPO'. The rough ER card was also wrong in science: proteins do not travel from the nucleus to the Golgi along the ER; ribosomes on the rough ER make them and the ER carries them on. Using one mapping everywhere stops learners having to unlearn one version.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 4.4 'The endomembrane system and proteins'
records.group_headline: The Kenyan analogies were mapped differently in Lessons 3 and 5 (nucleus, Golgi, membrane, rough ER) and their limits were never stated; both now match and limits are named

records.old: it produces the instructions (rRNA) for making ribosomes.'
records.new: it produces the instructions (rRNA) for making ribosomes.' For each analogy also say aloud where it breaks down: the jiko BURNS charcoal, but mitochondria do not burn food — they release its energy in many small, controlled steps and store it in ATP, and the cristae are folds that increase surface for these reactions; the governor's office has people who decide, but the nucleus only holds the instructions (DNA) that the cell reads; the GPO and the roads move parcels with vehicles, but proteins move in small membrane bubbles (vesicles); a port gate checks everything, but the cell membrane lets water and small molecules such as oxygen cross freely while controlling larger ones. Two structures on the Key have no analogy, so state their jobs directly: centrioles help organise the fibres that separate chromosomes when an animal cell divides, and smooth ER makes lipids (fats) and, in liver cells, helps remove poisons.
records.why: Guideline 6 asks that each analogy's limits are stated. Only the teacher reflection mentioned one risk (that mitochondria 'burn' food). Limits are now named for each analogy. Centrioles and smooth ER are on the observation task and the Lesson 3 model colour-coding but were never given a function, so one sentence each is added.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 4.3-4.5 (mitochondria, endomembrane system, centrosome and centrioles)

records.old: That is why the folded membranes — which are only a few nanometres thick — are invisible under the light microscope.'
records.new: That is why the folded membranes — which are only a few nanometres thick — are invisible under the light microscope.' Be accurate with learners: chloroplasts (the green granules, about 5 micrometres) and often the large vacuole can be seen with a good light microscope. What our school slide misses is mainly (i) tiny structures (membranes about 7 nm thick, ribosomes about 25 nm) and (ii) low contrast, because a fresh unstained hand-cut section is thick and clear; mitochondria (about 1 micrometre) are close to the limit of a light microscope. The electron microscope shows all of these clearly on a thin, stained slice.
records.why: Teachers chose this phenomenon, and it is kept. But as written it says the fluid-filled space and oval bodies are 'visible only under the electron microscope'. A light microscope can show a large plant vacuole, and mitochondria are near its resolving limit (about 200 nm); in a school slide they are missed mostly because of thickness and low contrast. Numbers checked: light microscope resolution about 200 nm; thylakoid membrane about 7 nm; ribosome about 25 nm; mitochondrion about 0.5 to 1 micrometre; chloroplast about 3 to 10 micrometres. The teacher decides how much of this nuance to give Grade 10 learners.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 4.1 'Studying cells' (resolution, light versus electron microscopes) and Chapter 4.3
records.group_headline: The explanation said the big vacuole and mitochondria are invisible to the light microscope only because of resolution; the truth is size plus faint contrast, so the explanation is made accurate while keeping the teachers' phenomenon

records.old: 'Can you see any folded membrane structures inside the large oval body near the centre?'
records.new: 'Can you see any folded membrane structures inside the small oval bodies scattered in the cytoplasm?'
records.why: The large oval body near the centre is the nucleus, which does not contain folded inner membranes. The folded inner membranes (cristae) are inside the mitochondria, the small oval bodies. As written, the prompt could lead learners to the wrong organelle. Checked against the second prompt, which calls the large dark oval near the centre the nucleus.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 4.3 (mitochondria and cristae, nucleus)

records.old: Set a 7-minute timer. Circulate actively, listening for misconceptions. When you hear a misconception, do NOT correct it immediately. Does the function card match that?' After 7 minutes, say: 'Now find another pair near you — groups of four. Compare your matches. Where you disagree, use your Lesson 3 and 4 notes to argue for your answer. You have 4 minutes.'

records.old: Groups spend 12 minutes filling in: (a) a specific Kenyan example at each level for both organisms (e.g., chloroplast / mitochondrion → leaf cell / muscle cell → mesophyll tissue / muscle tissue → leaf / stomach → shoot system / digestive system → sukuma wiki plant / human being), (b) a linking phrase on each arrow explaining HOW the lower level builds the higher (e.g., 'Many leaf cells with aligned chloroplasts form mesophyll tissue, which maximises light capture for photosynthesis'), and (c) one function that ONLY the higher level can perform that the lower level cannot. After group construction, the class does a 5-minute gallery walk: each group posts their map on the wall, and every learner places one green sticky-note (something scientifically correct and specific) and one yellow sticky-note (a question or suggested improvement) on two other groups' maps. Groups then return to their own map for 2 minutes to revise based on feedback. The teacher facilitates a 5-minute whole-class debrief, cold-calling groups to defend specific linking phrases.

After group construction, the class does a 4-minute gallery walk: each group posts their map on the wall, and every learner places one green sticky-note (something scientifically correct and specific) and one yellow sticky-note (a question or suggested improvement) on two other groups' maps. Groups then return to their own map for 1 minute to revise based on feedback. The teacher facilitates a 3-minute whole-class debrief, cold-calling groups to defend specific linking phrases.

records.old: Part 1 — Collaborative class explanation (7 minutes): Class reconvenes. Teacher projects the original anchoring phenomenon image alongside the DQB. Using a structured whole-class co-construction strategy, the teacher builds a paragraph on the board sentence by sentence, cold-calling individual learners to contribute. The paragraph answers the question: 'Why does the sukuma wiki leaf stay alive, and what happens inside its cells when it wilts and dries?' Learners must use evidence from their 7-lesson journey: organelle names and functions, plant-cell-specific structures, and at least one level of organisation. Learners copy the completed paragraph into their books. Part 2 — Individual performance task (8 minutes): Teacher distributes a printed or projected photomicrograph of a plant cell (sukuma wiki or spinach cell electron micrograph, clearly showing nucleus, chloroplasts, cell wall, vacuole, mitochondria, cell membrane, and endoplasmic reticulum). Each learner individually: (i) draws and labels the cell, identifying at least six organelles; (ii) writes a paragraph (minimum 4 sentences) explaining how the structures they have labelled work together to keep the plant cell — and therefore the whole sukuma wiki plant — alive. Teacher circulates and asks targeted probing questions to individual learners. Learners submit the performance task at the end of the lesson for teacher review.

The paragraph answers the question: 'Why does the sukuma wiki leaf stay alive, and what happens inside its cells when it wilts and dries?' Learners must use evidence from their 7-lesson journey: organelle names and functions, plant-cell-specific structures, and at least one level of organisation. Learners copy the completed paragraph into their books. Part 2 — Individual performance task (10 minutes): Teacher distributes a printed or projected photomicrograph of a plant cell (sukuma wiki or spinach cell electron micrograph, clearly showing nucleus, chloroplasts, cell wall, vacuole, mitochondria, cell membrane, and endoplasmic reticulum). Each learner individually: (i) draws and labels the cell, identifying at least six organelles; (ii) writes a paragraph (minimum 4 sentences) explaining how the structures they have labelled work together to keep the plant cell — and therefore the whole sukuma wiki plant — alive. Teacher circulates and asks targeted probing questions to individual learners. Learners submit the performance task at the end of the lesson for teacher review. Learners who find extended writing difficult may explain their diagram aloud to the teacher or a partner, or use a flow diagram with arrows and short labels instead of a paragraph; learners may note key terms in Kiswahili first and then write in English.
records.why: The individual performance task asks learners to draw and label a plant cell with six or more organelles and write a paragraph of four sentences or more in 8 minutes, which is too tight, while the co-written class paragraph took 7. Swapped to 5 and 10; the 15-minute Explain phase and the 40-minute total are unchanged. Also adds more than one way to show understanding (guideline 12).

records.old: Notice we are writing the way scientists write — claim, evidence, reason.'
records.new: Notice we are writing the way scientists write — claim, evidence, reasoning. The CLAIM is the answer to our question (for example, 'the leaf wilts because its cells lose water'). The EVIDENCE is what we observed (the fresh and wilted leaf, the micrographs, and the Observed and Learned rows of our Summary Tables from Lessons 1 to 7). The REASONING is the science idea that links them (the vacuole loses water, turgor pressure falls, and the cell wall alone cannot hold the leaf up).'
records.why: The words 'claim, evidence, reason' were used without a definition, and the Summary Tables were never used to build the final explanation (guideline 7). Definitions follow the standard: claim = answer, evidence = data or observations, reasoning = the science idea linking them.

records.new: small maize grains or beads (ribosomes; larger grains or bean seeds painted green can stand for chloroplasts), bean seeds (mitochondria or nucleus)

records.old: Wash hands after handling clay.
records.new: Wash hands after handling clay. If painting seeds, use water-based poster paint or markers, let them dry, and do not put any material in the mouth. If maize, beans or clay are not available, use bottle tops, pebbles, beads, paper balls, dry leaves or thread instead; the model works as long as each choice is justified.

records.old: knowing the name means nothing if you do not know the job.'
records.new: knowing the name means nothing if you do not know the job.' Language support: write the Kiswahili word next to each English word on the board (for example seli = cell, hadubini = microscope, kiini = nucleus, utando wa seli = cell membrane, ukuta wa seli = cell wall, saitoplazimu = cytoplasm) and invite learners to add words from their home languages. For learners with low vision give enlarged A3 prints; learners who find writing difficult can name and point to structures aloud while a partner records.
records.why: The unit had no language support for English learners and few accommodations. The Kiswahili terms are standard biology terms as I know them, but I cannot verify them against the school's textbook, so a Kiswahili teacher must confirm them before use.

records.old: • A maize (corn) grain soaked in water overnight swells noticeably; learners observe thin cross-sections under the light microscope and see that individual cells have increased in size — this anchors inquiry into the large central vacuole of plant cells and its role in water uptake.
records.new: • A wilted piece of sukuma wiki left in clean water for an hour becomes firm and crisp again — the cells have taken in water, their vacuoles have refilled and turgor pressure has returned; this anchors inquiry into the large central vacuole of plant cells and shows that wilting is reversible when the cells have not yet died.
records.why: A dry maize grain swells mainly by soaking up water into its stored starch and protein (imbibition); its cells do not have a large central vacuole, so the old phenomenon did not support the claim made about vacuoles. A wilted leaf recovering in water is a standard classroom demonstration of turgor, uses the same sukuma wiki leaf as the anchor, and connects directly to the anchor phenomenon. The teacher decides whether to keep this swap.
records.reference: OpenStax Biology 2e (2018), Chapter 5.2 'Passive transport' (osmosis, tonicity) and Chapter 30 (turgor pressure)
records.group_headline: One supporting phenomenon (soaked maize grain 'cells swell') was scientifically wrong and never used; replaced by a wilted leaf recovering in water, which now appears in Lesson 4

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clearly links the different pictures to resolution and magnification, using the correct values or comparisons, and names two further differences correctly.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Says the electron microscope shows more detail and gives one or two correct differences, but without clear reference to resolution.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States that one microscope is better, with no correct scientific reason or differences.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Accurate, neat labelled plant cell with eight or more correct labels and correct plant versus animal differences.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Mostly accurate diagram with five to seven correct labels and at least two correct differences.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Diagram is incomplete or has several wrong labels and the differences are mostly incorrect.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives correct functions for five organelles and explains how at least two depend on each other, using Kenyan examples.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives correct functions for most organelles and mentions a link between them.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives few correct functions and does not show how organelles work together.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives a full, correctly ordered cause-and-effect chain: water loss, shrinking vacuole and lost turgor (the wilting), then slower photosynthesis and energy release as the cells dry out, then death of cells, tissues and the leaf; also explains the green colour and crispness.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains wilting using water loss and turgor, with some later steps (photosynthesis, energy release, cell death) missing or out of order.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Only says the leaf dies because it dries, with no reference to cell structures.

value.criterion: Levels of organisation and answering the driving question
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Orders all six levels correctly, gives correct examples for both organisms, and answers the driving question using evidence.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Orders the levels with one or two errors and gives a partly complete answer.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Levels are mostly wrongly ordered and the answer to the driving question is missing or unrelated.

records.why: The level names (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches Expectations) now appear in each descriptor, as the printed headings cannot be changed. The 'explaining the phenomenon' descriptors now follow the corrected order of causes (water loss and lost turgor first); the old 'turgor OR photosynthesis' wording let a learner who gave only photosynthesis reach 'Meets'.

records.why: The CBE level 'Below Expectations' cannot be represented: the contract allows only three level fields. Suggestion: keep the descriptors as they are and let the teacher record 'Below Expectations' in the mark sheet for work that does not meet even the Approaches Expectations descriptor; confirm with the partner whether a fourth field can be added.

No KICD General Science curriculum PDF is available, so the learning outcomes (a to f), key inquiry question and competencies could not be checked against KICD wording and have been left unchanged. The closest KICD source is Grade 10 Biology, Strand 1.0 Cell Biology and Biodiversity, Sub-Strand 1.3 Cell Structure and Specialisation (outcomes: differentiate light and electron microscopes; prepare temporary slides and estimate cell size; describe plant and animal cells under the electron microscope; relate specialised cells to function; appreciate the cell as the basic unit of life; key inquiry questions 'Why do plant and animal cells differ?' and 'How are cells specialised?'). Differences noted: this unit has the number 1.2 and the name 'The Cell' (KICD Biology uses 1.3 and a different title); it teaches levels of organisation and a concept map (in the Biology outcomes only as a content bullet); and it does not teach slide preparation with cell-size estimation or specialised cells, which Biology includes. Teachers should confirm the General Science source wording.
